topIssues.title: Telegram system-bot onboarding is dead and does not bind Cloud identity
topIssues.author: lalalune
topIssues.body:
## Contribution provenance

AI assistance is self-reported provenance, not a request for hidden reasoning. No secrets, one-time pairing tokens, private session IDs, or hidden prompts are included below.

- AI assistance: yes
- AI provider/model: OpenAI / gpt-5.6-sol
- Client / agent tooling: Codex desktop
- Contribution skill revision: elizaOS/eliza@403dd7a7eb253000fe89be7319e0425c3bf33b6e:packages/skills/skills/contribute-to-eliza
- Attribution status: self-reported

**Describe the bug**

The production system Telegram bot can receive a first-contact DM and return an onboarding URL, but the URL points at `https://eliza.app/get-started`, which currently fails to boot reliably. Even when the same one-time onboarding path is moved to the authenticated `https://app.elizacloud.ai/get-started` host as a diagnostic workaround, it does not durably bind the Telegram sender identity to the signed-in Cloud account. A subsequent DM receives the onboarding response again instead of reaching the account's assigned agent.

This breaks the required handoff:

`Telegram sender -> signed-in Eliza Cloud account -> that account's assigned agent -> reply through the same Telegram conversation`

**Root causes observed**

1. `packages/cloud/api/wrangler.toml` overrides `ELIZA_ONBOARDING_APP_URL` to `https://eliza.app`, although the application default points to `https://app.elizacloud.ai`.
2. The waitlist deployment replaced the prior full Eliza Vite application on `eliza.app`. A production browser request for the referenced main JavaScript asset with `Origin: https://eliza.app` returned cached HTML (`text/html`), so the browser rejected it as a module. The same asset request without that Origin returned JavaScript, demonstrating inconsistent cache/fallback behavior rather than a missing local browser capability.
3. The generic one-time onboarding/pair flow does not complete the signed Telegram identity proof required for durable `telegram` external-identity linking. A successful browser sign-in alone must not be treated as proof that the browser account owns an arbitrary Telegram sender ID.

**To reproduce**

1. From a Telegram account that is not yet linked, DM the production system bot `@IamEliza_bot`.
2. Observe that the bot receives the DM and returns a one-time `eliza.app/get-started` URL.
3. Open the URL in a production browser. Observe the empty app shell / module MIME failure.
4. As a diagnostic only, open the same unexpired one-time path on the authenticated `app.elizacloud.ai` host.
5. After the flow redirects, send a second DM asking the assigned agent to reply.
6. Observe that the bot sends the first-contact onboarding response again instead of routing the message to the account's assigned agent.

Do not paste the one-time onboarding token, account email, Telegram numeric sender ID, or agent UUID into public evidence.

**Expected behavior**

- The bot's onboarding URL loads on a canonical supported application host.
- An authenticated user completes a Telegram-signed identity handoff (for example, Telegram Login/OAuth signed payload validated server-side) before the external identity is linked.
- The linked identity is persisted using the canonical Telegram provider and sender identifier.
- The next DM resolves the same Cloud user, routes to that user's assigned agent, and returns the agent response through the same Telegram conversation.
- Expired, replayed, mismatched, or unsigned attempts fail explicitly and cannot link another person's Telegram identity.
- If a signed-in user has no agent, the existing connector onboarding path creates or assigns one before completing the link.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ] `ELIZA_ONBOARDING_APP_URL` resolves to a host that serves a working `/get-started` application and its immutable assets with correct content types and cache behavior.
- [ ] The Telegram handoff includes server-validated Telegram proof; browser authentication alone is insufficient.
- [ ] External-identity persistence and any gateway caches agree immediately after linking.
- [ ] A real first DM returns onboarding once; after successful linking, a real second DM reaches the user's assigned agent.
- [ ] The agent's response is delivered to the same Telegram conversation.
- [ ] Negative E2E cases cover expired link, replay, sender mismatch, unsigned/invalid Telegram payload, signed-in user without an agent, and already-linked identity conflict.
- [ ] Evidence includes redacted gateway/API logs and the resulting identity/agent routing record without exposing secrets or stable private identifiers.

**Screenshots / recording of the wrong behavior (required for anything visible)**

N/A - the failure was inspected live, but the browser URL contains a one-time credential and the signed-in page contains private account and agent identifiers. Public capture must be redacted before attachment.

**Evidence / reproduction proof**

- [ ] N/A - MP4/JPG withheld because the live page exposes one-time and account identifiers; attach a purpose-built redacted capture during implementation verification.
- [ ] Production browser console/network evidence observed: the main module request was served as `text/html` with Origin and rejected; attach a redacted HAR/console excerpt during verification.
- [ ] N/A - no real-LLM trajectory is needed to establish this identity/onboarding transport failure; live agent trajectory is required for the final positive acceptance run.
- [ ] Production domain artifact observed: two consecutive DMs returned onboarding instead of the second DM resolving to the assigned agent; attach redacted identity/route records during verification.

**Additional context**

The Telegram gateway transport itself is alive: production received the DM and delivered the onboarding reply. The failure is specifically the canonical application handoff plus durable, provider-authenticated identity binding. A URL-host correction is a useful immediate repair but is not sufficient by itself to satisfy secure Telegram account linking.

— [codex-gateway]

topIssues.title: prod: fleet-wide agent provisioning outage — CI runner farm saturates eliza-core-prod-1 IO, every docker create times out
topIssues.author: standujar
topIssues.body:
## Impact

**No new agent has provisioned anywhere on the fleet since 2026-08-06 ~11:41 UTC.** Every `agent_provision` job either failed (`Job timed out 3 times - max attempts reached`, 8 jobs) or is currently grinding through its retries (3 jobs). Telegram/eliza-app onboarding creates the sandbox row, then the container never arrives — the user stays on "your container is provisioning" forever.

Existing agents are unaffected (heartbeats healthy fleet-wide).

## Root cause — measured on the node, 2026-08-07 00:30–00:45 UTC

`eliza-core-prod-1` (88.99.66.168) is both a production agent node **and** the self-hosted GitHub Actions farm: 22 `actions-runner@N` services, 11 concurrent `Runner.Worker` jobs churning `elizaOS/eliza` workflows, on a SATA RAID-1.

The CI concurrency saturates the disks, and container creation — which needs journal flushes — can no longer complete inside the provisioner's 60s command timeout:

```
load average: 451.39, 356.19, 208.83          (machine sized for 16 agent containers)
/proc/pressure/io  full avg60=78.50           (the box spends ~80% of time stalled on IO)
disk util over a 4s sample: sda 78%, sdb 72%  (sustained, with ~39 MB/s writes)

366 processes in D-state:
    224  runc:[2:INIT]   flush_workqueue      <- container creates piled up
    116  runc            flush_workqueue
     10  tar             jbd2_log_do_checkpoint   cwd = /opt/actions-runners/runner-N/_work/eliza/eliza
      1  md2_raid1       md_super_wait

256 runc processes total, ages 16s → 21min — churning, not deadlocked: every
container create takes minutes instead of seconds.
```

The RAID itself is healthy (`[UU]`, no resync, no ATA errors in dmesg). The box has been in this state since yesterday morning: `systemd-journald` has been dying on its watchdog since **Aug 6 12:51** (it cannot fsync in time), right after the first provision timeout at 11:41.

## Why it kills the whole fleet, not one node

Every other node is over its declared capacity (see #17866), so the placement selector picks the only node with free slots — this one — for **every** provision:

```
[docker-node-manager] Selected node eliza-core-prod-1 (14/16 used)
[docker-sandbox] Pulling image ... Image pulled successfully        <- pull OK (11s)
[docker-sandbox] Registering ... with Steward tenant ...            <- OK
[docker-ssh] Command timed out after 60000ms on 88.99.66.168: docker ...   <- create dies
```

Each failed attempt also leaves a half-created container behind, which the replacement-cleanup reconciler then refuses to remove (`Replacement attempt label mismatch` — the guard is doing its job) or times out on, so two agents (`d6e37e91`, `f27f096d`) are stuck in a permanent cleanup loop on top of the outage.

## Remediation

Immediate (ops, needs an operator on the node):
1. Pause the runner farm on this node (`systemctl stop 'actions-runner@*'`) until IO pressure drains — in-flight CI jobs get killed and are re-runnable. Docker recovers on its own once the runc backlog flushes; the stuck `agent_provision` jobs retry automatically via the watchdog.
2. Longer term: CI runners and production agent placement should not share a spindle-backed box. Either move the farm, or fence its IO (systemd `IOWeight`/cgroup io.max), or remove this node from the placement pool.

Code-side hardening (separate PRs):
3. Per-node circuit breaker in the placement selector: a node whose docker commands repeatedly time out should be quarantined for a cooldown instead of being re-selected for every subsequent provision (it is the sole "free" node precisely when the fleet is saturated — the worst moment to hammer it).
4. The stranded label-mismatch containers need a bounded resolution path rather than an endless reconcile loop.

Related: #17866 (fleet over declared capacity — why this node is always selected).

topIssues.title: gitleaks PR scan uses a two-dot range and flags files the PR never touched
topIssues.author: lalalune
topIssues.body:
## Summary

`.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml:72` scopes the pull-request scan with a **two-dot** range:

```bash
RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}..${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
```

`github.event.pull_request.base.sha` is the base branch tip **at event time**, not the merge base. So on any branch that has merged `develop` (or was opened against an older base), `base..head` includes commits the branch merely *inherited* — and gitleaks scans files the PR never touched.

## Observed

PR #17420 failed `gitleaks` on findings in
`packages/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro/helper_code/sweap_eval_full_v2.jsonl` (lines 111, 149) — Go module checksums (`h1:` hashes out of a `go.sum`), matched by `generic-api-key`. They are content hashes of public modules, not secrets.

That file is not in the PR at all:

```
$ gh pr view 17420 --json files --jq '.files[].path' | grep swe-bench-pro
  (no output)

$ git ls-tree origin/develop packages/benchmarks/swe-bench-pro/helper_code/sweap_eval_full_v2.jsonl
  (no output — not on develop either)

$ mb=$(git merge-base origin/develop <head>)
$ git diff --name-only "$mb" <head> | grep swe-bench-pro
  (no output)
```

So a PR is blocked by a finding in a file it does not touch, that is not on the target branch, and that is not in its merge-base..head diff.

## Fix

Use a three-dot range, which git resolves to `merge-base(base, head)..head`:

```diff
           if [[ "$EVENT_NAME" == "pull_request" ]]; then
-            RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}..${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
+            # Three-dot: scan merge-base(base,head)..head, i.e. only what THIS
+            # PR added. `pull_request.base.sha` is the base branch tip at event
+            # time, not the merge base, so a two-dot range also scans commits the
+            # branch merely inherited by merging develop — re-flagging fixtures
+            # the PR never touched.
+            RANGE_ARGS=(--log-opts "${PR_BASE_SHA}...${PR_HEAD_SHA}")
           elif [[ -n "$BEFORE_SHA" && ... ]]; then
```

This is the same lesson the evidence gate already learned. `.github/workflows/develop-pr.yml` scopes its changed-file diff with an explicit comment:

> `# Three-dot: diff the merge-base..head, i.e. only what THIS PR changed,`
> `# not files the base branch advanced past the branch point (#16125).`

and uses `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=ACMRT "$BASE_SHA...$HEAD_SHA"`. Gitleaks is the remaining two-dot consumer of the same pair.

The `push` branches (`BEFORE_SHA..CURRENT_SHA`, and the orphan/root and tip-commit cases below) are correct as-is — this only concerns the `pull_request` arm.

## Why I did not open a PR

The change touches `.github/workflows/`, which needs a token with `workflow` scope; my pushes are refused with

```
refusing to allow an OAuth App to create or update workflow `.github/workflows/gitleaks.yml` without `workflow` scope
```

The patch above is complete and applies cleanly to current `develop`.

## Impact

Every PR whose branch has merged `develop` is exposed to false-positive secret findings from unrelated history, and the failure blocks `Develop PR Gate` since gitleaks is a required component. It also trains reviewers to wave through red gitleaks results, which is the more expensive long-term cost.

topIssues.title: planner: failed-step turns reply with a canned "runtime step failed" line instead of describing what actually failed
topIssues.author: NubsCarson
topIssues.body:
## Summary
When a planner step fails and the turn ends without a usable result, the user-facing reply is a fixed canned sentence from `packages/core/src/runtime/planner-loop.ts`: "I tried to complete that, but the available runtime step failed before it produced a usable result." The failure's human-readable cause is available at that point but never reaches the reply, so the user gets an opaque internal-sounding sentence — the same leak class fixed for orchestrator surfaces in #17923, but in the core planner reply path.

## Live example (2026-08-07 12:10Z)
User: "Look at this weeks progress" → planner correctly chose SHELL → `git log --since="1 week ago" --oneline` → exit 128 (`fatal: your current branch 'master' does not have any commits yet` — the agent workspace root is a commit-less init'd repo; the real checkout lives elsewhere) → reply: the canned line. An honest reply was one sentence away: "tried to check the git log but my workspace repo has no commits."

Trajectory: 1 planner iteration, 1 tool call, 1 failure, FINISH→CONTINUE, 4,956ms — the machinery all worked; only the final wording discards the context.

## Suggested structural fix
Feed the failed step's error summary (the tool result's `text`/typed error message, already human-shaped after #17923-style producers) into the final-reply prompt context so the model can state what failed and why, instead of substituting a fixed sentence. Secondary (separate concern): after a failed step the planner could attempt one alternative (different cwd/repo for VCS queries) before concluding.

topPRs.title: fix(plugin-wallet): honor confirmed slippage in EVM swap/bridge execution
topPRs.author: SashaMIT
topPRs.body:
## Summary

A swap you confirmed at 0.1% slippage could still execute at 2%: the EVM swap and bridge paths accepted `slippageBps` at the wallet router, bound it into the confirmation pending key, and then silently dropped it before quoting.

Three drop points lined up:

1. `executeSwap` (both the chain-handler and registry EVM paths) called `SwapAction.swap` without `params.slippageBps`, so `SwapAction` always walked its 1% -> 1.5% -> 2% escalation ladder. A user who confirmed tighter than 2% could still execute at 2% (20x for a 0.1% confirmation).
2. Both `routeEvmBridge` call sites (prepare quote and execute) reach `BridgeAction.getQuote`, which hardcoded `DEFAULT_SLIPPAGE_PERCENT` (1%) regardless of the confirmed value.
3. `slippageBps` has been bound in `walletFinancialPendingKey` all along, so the confirm turn promised parameter integrity that the execution layer did not deliver. Severity is bounded (max 2% on swap, fixed 1% on bridge), but it is a confirm-vs-execute integrity break in the same class the pending key was built to prevent.

Sibling of #18003 and #18006 (same wallet confirmation-integrity pass).

## Fix

- `chains/evm/types`: `SwapParams` and `BridgeParams` gain optional `slippageBps`.
- `chains/evm/chain-handler.ts` and `chains/registry.ts`: both EVM swap execution sites forward `params.slippageBps` to `SwapAction.swap`.
- `chains/evm/actions/swap.ts`: when `slippageBps` is set, the quote ladder collapses to exactly that tolerance (`slippageBps / 10000` as the Li.Fi slippage fraction); the 1% -> 1.5% -> 2% escalation now runs only when no slippage was stated, so a confirmed value is never exceeded.
- `chains/evm/bridge-router.ts`: `BridgeAction.getQuote` converts confirmed `slippageBps` to the Li.Fi slippage fraction and keeps `DEFAULT_SLIPPAGE_PERCENT` as the unstated fallback; `routeEvmBridge` forwards the param on both the prepare quote and the execute call.
- `security/wallet-financial-confirmation.ts`: `walletFinancialPreview` now discloses the authorized slippage in swap and bridge confirmation prompts (`Swap 1 ETH to USDC on base with up to 0.1% slippage (10 bps)?`), so a 10 bps and a 10,000 bps confirmation no longer read identically. Prompts with no stated slippage are labeled `with default slippage`: the unstated default is not one chain-agnostic number (EVM swaps escalate 1% -> 1.5% -> 2%, bridges hold 1%, Solana is dynamic). (Review follow-up, thanks @HomunculusLabs.)
- `chains/evm/types`: `SwapParamsSchema` and `BridgeParamsSchema` now accept and bounds-check optional `slippageBps` (`z.coerce.number().int().min(0).max(10_000)`, mirroring the wallet-router boundary), closing the latent parse-layer drop point where the field was silently stripped.

Unchanged because it already works: the Solana swap path honors `params.slippageBps` end to end.

## Test plan

- [x] Maintainer exact-head validation (`2680a2d`): 11/11 regression tests; full wallet suite 260 passed / 1 skipped; plugin-wallet and app-core typechecks pass; root verify 346/346 tasks plus all audits.
- [x] New regression suite `plugins/plugin-wallet/src/chains/evm/__tests__/unit/slippage-threading.test.ts` (6 tests): the router forwards confirmed `slippageBps` to `SwapAction.swap`; swap quotes at exactly 10 bps (0.001) when confirmed; swap keeps the 1% default first quote when unstated; bridge execute quotes at exactly 50 bps (0.005) when confirmed; bridge keeps the 1% default when unstated; the prepare-mode bridge quote threads the confirmed value too.
- [x] Red run from parent-commit source (`d72e9e4`): 4 failed, 2 passed (the two default-preservation tests pass on both sides, as designed).
- [x] Green run with the fix: 6 passed.

topPRs.title: fix(plugin-elizacloud): retry cold-gateway warming 503 in place instead of consuming the failover ladder
topPRs.author: NubsCarson
topPRs.body:
A cold Cloudflare Worker answers the first request after idle with a 503 carrying a structural `*_cache_warming` code (`auth_cache_warming`, `rate_limit_cache_warming`, `inference_dependency_cache_warming`, `billing_cache_warming`) while it hydrates its caches. The container treated that 503 as a hard provider failure: the runtime `useModel` failover ladder classifies any thrown 503 as fallback-class and advances instantly, so the whole `RESPONSE_HANDLER -> TEXT_NANO -> TEXT_SMALL -> TEXT_LARGE` ladder was spent in ~83ms while real gateway recovery is 1,000-1,410ms. Measured baseline: the first turn after idle FAILED 4/4 with a canned error delivered at 3,800-4,600ms.

## Fix

Gate on the structural status+code shape (never message prose) and retry the same request in place with a bounded backoff schedule (250/500/1000/1500ms; `Retry-After` respected up to a 2s cap), across both buffered routes and the streaming path. Any other 503 body, any non-503 status, non-JSON 503 bodies, and network errors still throw immediately, so genuine outages keep failing over promptly.

## Production capture

The warming 503 was captured from the live gateway three times: the billing lane after a 40-minute natural idle (cf-ray `a271385cde41b15f-BOS`, 2026-08-06 21:43:58 UTC) and the auth lane induced (cf-ray `a27147c469398fb5-BOS`). The full capture is pasted in the Evidence Gate below.

## Bench proof (differential harness, captured prod 503 body replayed by a local server)

Adversarial-review bench: old code threw all 4 ladder rungs in 83ms and failed the turn; new code succeeded at 3,283ms buffered / 3,314ms streaming against a 3,000ms recovery window, and 784ms/763ms for a realistic 600ms recovery. Retry budget is 3,250ms vs measured production recovery of 1,000-1,410ms = 3.5x margin.

Fresh re-run of the same harness at this head (109f7ef9e23):

- 3,000ms recovery: OLD exhausted all 4 rungs in 9ms and the turn failed; NEW first rung succeeded at 3,370ms buffered / 3,293ms streaming — ladder never consumed.
- 600ms recovery: OLD exhausted in 53ms and failed; NEW succeeded at 791ms buffered / 780ms streaming.
- Inverse: a real provider 503 (`api_error`) threw in 1ms with a single attempt — the ladder is preserved for real outages.

Real failures fail fast at +0ms in every class: non-503 status, 503 with a non-warming code, non-JSON 503 body, network error (all pinned in the new unit suite).

## Caveats (stated plainly — adversarial review verdict: SHIP WITH CAVEAT)

- (a) The fixed container has never contacted the real gateway: the image build is blocked by the GitHub Actions outage. The post-deploy first-turn-after-idle test is MANDATORY before trusting this in production.
- (b) The `/responses` path change is dead code against the currently deployed worker (it never emits the warming shape on that route today).
- (c) A sustained warming outage now costs ~15-19s before the canned error instead of ~0.5s — that is the deliberate price of surviving the normal 1-1.4s warm-up.

## Local CI (GitHub Actions major outage)

GitHub Actions is in a major outage, so the suites CI would run for the touched package were executed locally at this head (109f7ef9e23, on top of develop c43d283cf5d) in `/home/milady/iqlabs/.compose-fix-wt`. Exact counts:

topPRs.title: fix(plugin-wallet): bind bridge recipient guard and show destination in confirmation preview
topPRs.author: SashaMIT
topPRs.body:
## Summary

A bridge recipient injected into planner parameters (the GHSA-7qxr-x6cg-r9cc class) got bridged to after a blind "yes": the recipient-authorization guard wrapped only `transfer`, and the bridge confirmation preview never showed where the funds go.

Two gaps lined up in the wallet router:

1. The GHSA-7qxr-x6cg-r9cc recipient guard in `runWalletRouter` fired only for `params.subaction === "transfer"`. `routeEvmBridge` maps `params.recipient` to the Li.Fi destination `toAddress` (`chains/evm/bridge-router.ts`), so a recipient absent from the user message sailed through for `bridge`.
2. The bridge confirmation preview was `Bridge {amount} from {chain} to {toChain}?`, omitting the recipient (and the token), while the transfer preview shows `to {recipient}`. The pending key already binds `recipient`, so the user was confirming a value they never saw.

Follow-up to #17773 and #17775 (same GHSA-7qxr / GHSA-gh63 lineage).

## Fix

- `chains/wallet-action.ts`: the recipient guard now covers `bridge` with the same semantics as `transfer` (EVM and Solana address forms, same rejection channel).
- `security/wallet-financial-confirmation.ts`: the bridge preview is now `Bridge {amount} {fromToken} from {chain} to {toChain} to {recipient}? ...`. With no recipient set it reads `Bridge {amount} {fromToken} from {chain} to {toChain}? ...`, matching the Li.Fi default of returning funds to the sender on the destination chain.

## Known limitation (planner-path guard vacuity, follow-up)

Stated plainly so this fix is not misread: in the planner path, `options.parameters` IS the LLM tool-call output (`packages/core/src/runtime/execute-planned-tool-call.ts`), and `collectExplicitRecipients` treats those parameters as user authorization. The recipient guard (transfer before, and now bridge) therefore authorizes the LLM's own params against themselves in that flow; it only bites for content-driven invocations that carry no structured options. Making the guard non-vacuous in the planner path means distinguishing user-supplied parameters from planner output at the confirmation boundary, a core-runtime change best done as its own PR. The load-bearing user-facing control this PR adds for bridge is the other half: the confirmation preview discloses the exact destination, and the pending key binds it, so a recipient swapped after the prompt produces a fresh confirmation instead of executing.

## Test plan

- [x] New regression suite `plugins/plugin-wallet/src/chains/__tests__/wallet-bridge-recipient.test.ts` (5 tests): content-driven bridge with unstated recipient rejected; stated recipient accepted and pends confirmation; preview shows the destination and the confirmed bridge executes after "yes"; self-bridge preview carries no destination clause; transfer rejection parity holds.
- [x] Red run from parent-commit source (`d72e9e4`): 3 failed, 2 passed (guard missing, preview hid the recipient).
- [x] Green run with the fix: 5 passed.
- [x] Full plugin-wallet suite: 231 passed, 1 skipped. The `api/wallet-routes` and `ui/InventoryView` test files fail identically on a clean checkout (unrelated import-resolution errors, same pair as noted in #17773).
- [x] `bunx biome check --write` on the changed files: clean, no fixes applied.
- [x] Typecheck: `bun run typecheck` fails identically on pristine parent source in this clone (`@elizaos/core` workspace types not built, TS2307 in `src/wallet/*.ts`); the diff introduces no new errors.

topPRs.title: fix(ui): recover the join flow from a stale binding to a deleted agent
topPRs.author: NubsCarson
topPRs.body:
> Publication sync (2026-08-06): exact head `149437f056ae97d827b74797d4cf4d768cc92811` is one scoped commit above merged `develop@acf5fe75b4e95fef33710f5003101abd74f521cc`. The original patch is preserved and the sole reviewer follow-up now reuses the shared agent-gone classifier. Exact-head frozen install, 33/33 UI tests, 31/31 LifeOps tests, targeted Biome, and full 343/343 root verification pass; refreshed CI is rerunning after a GitHub Actions service outage. Exact-head desktop and mobile join-surface audits passed 2/2 with zero broken or needs-work findings; the recovery screenshots/video remain explicitly labeled as behavioral-reference artifacts because the only post-capture semantic change is shared-classifier reuse.

Live user report tonight (staging): a browser holding a persisted agent binding to a **deleted** agent is permanently stuck on /join — every retry re-reads the dead binding, fires at the dead agent origin, gets the router's `404 {"error":"agent not found or not running"}`, and renders the terminal "Couldn't connect to your agent". The org actually had zero agents; the correct outcome was the create path.

Mechanism: the persisted `elizaos:active-server` binding points the client's base at `https://<agentId>.<env>.elizacloud.ai`; `selectOrProvisionCloudAgent`'s list step routes through that base, so *every* step of selection misroutes through the corpse.

Fix (structural, in the join controller): a new shared `isCloudAgentGoneError` classifier (404 + the router's structural agent-gone shape, cause-chain aware — transport failures never match); on agent-gone from a REMEMBERED binding, the flow clears the persisted binding, resets the client base to the fresh-visit control-plane path, and re-runs selection without the preference — zero agents → existing create path, agents exist → normal chooser. Real transport failures of a valid binding keep the existing terminal state. The LifeOps activity capture gets the same agent-gone shape added to its expected-degrade set (mirroring #17817's 401 pattern).
